title: Helping to Learn vs Teaching: Make Thinking Unavoidable
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: Drawing on Hector Ruiz Martin's How Do We Learn?, the author argues that busy, engaging classrooms are a poor proxy for learning because activity is behavioral while learning is cognitive. The central test is to ask what students are thinking about during a task, not what they are doing. A poster on the causes of the French Revolution serves as the example: students spend working memory on layout and division of labor instead of causation. The remedy is to design tasks where thinking about the content is unavoidable, such as ranking and defending causes. For practical implementation the author recommends Project Zero's Visible Thinking Routines and maps several of them onto familiar structures such as Do Nows, turn and talks, and mini whiteboards.
points: Activity is behavioral and learning is cognitive, so participation and completion are unreliable evidence that students are learning.
The diagnostic question for any task is what occupies students' working memory, not what they are doing or producing.
Posters and similar products can consume working memory on appearance and logistics, leaving little for the content and producing inert knowledge.
Tasks should be redesigned so the thinking required is the learning, for example by asking students to rank, defend, and connect causes.
Visible Thinking Routines can be layered onto existing structures like Think-Pair-Share, Do Nows and mini whiteboards to make thinking routine.
quotes: If we care about whether students actually learn in meaningful ways, we have to stop asking, “What are they doing?” and start asking, “What are they thinking about?” To put it bluntly: Learning is thinking. If students aren’t thinking, they aren’t learning.

We design “engaging” activities, group work, projects, posters, but do not fully consider whether those activities require students to think about the content in the ways necessary to promote meaningful learning.

That’s the illusion of active learning. Activity is behavioral. Learning is cognitive. And when those don’t align, you often get inert knowledge: stuff students “know” but never learned in ways that are durable and transferable.

They’re likely focused on what the title should look like, where to place images, how to divide the work, and how to make it look good. That’s all cognitive effort, but it’s the wrong kind. This leaves little working memory for meaningful thinking.
This is the activity problem: If students can complete the task without deeply thinking about the content, the task is flawed. In reality, it is a waste of time, effort, and resources.
So instead of asking students to create a poster, ask them to rank causes, defend their reasoning, and connect causes across contexts. Now they can’t just do the task. They have to think.

What I’ve found is that once students know the routines, implementation is very efficient. I don’t have to explain steps every time. I can just name the routine, and they know exactly what to do, and more importantly, why they’re doing it.
